claims.text: The initial conventionally sintered W–Cu composite contains discrete, isolated copper inclusions in a tungsten matrix.
Annealing below copper’s melting point can activate sufficient copper diffusion to promote copper coalescence at W–Cu interfaces.
Post-sintering annealing will cause isolated copper pockets to merge into continuous pathways.
The annealing treatment will form a continuous, percolating copper network within the tungsten matrix.
The interconnected copper network will lie along interfaces with the tungsten phase.
Formation of continuous copper pathways will reduce interfacial thermal resistance between copper and tungsten.
Reduced interfacial thermal resistance and increased copper connectivity will enhance effective heat conduction.
The annealed composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable as-sintered composite.
Isolated copper inclusions produce limited heat-conduction paths and lower overall thermal conductivity.
The baseline composite suffers from high interfacial thermal resistance.
The tungsten matrix has high strength and irradiation resistance.
The tungsten matrix will retain its structural integrity during the proposed annealing treatment.
Retention of tungsten-matrix integrity will maintain the composite’s mechanical durability and irradiation performance.
Yield strength and ductility after annealing will remain comparable to, or only slightly altered from, the as-sintered baseline.
Irradiation resistance after annealing will remain comparable to, or only slightly altered from, the as-sintered baseline.
Excessive annealing could cause tungsten grain growth, copper coarsening, loss of ductility, or degradation of the W–Cu bond.
The intervention is expected to succeed only when copper connectivity improves without detrimental changes to the tungsten matrix or irradiation resistance.
A thermal-conductivity improvement below 10% or a yield-strength decrease above 15% would falsify the hypothesis.
